Team, this is a short message before Thursday. You have all read the memo, so I will not repeat the numbers. I want to say one thing about how we decide. If we choose the first option, we protect the margin this year, but we lose volume in the south, and that is a real risk. If we choose the second one, we will need more people in the analytics team, and the result will not appear before the fourth quarter. Both options are defensible. What is not defensible is a decision with no argument behind it. So on Thursday, please come with a recommendation and one number that supports it. Thank you.

Good morning, and welcome to the session. Before we open the case, a word about how these discussions work here. In this room, I am not looking for the right answer. I am looking for your reasoning. So when I ask what you would do if you were the chief executive of this company, please do not tell me what the company actually did. Tell me what you would do, and tell me why. If you disagree with the person next to you, say so. The best sessions I have seen in twenty years of teaching were the ones where two people disagreed, and both of them were right about something. Let us begin.

First, the board reads the options memo. Then it compares the two scenarios in the meeting. After that, it chooses the option with the stronger argument. Next, the finance team allocates the budget for the first quarter. Finally, the company starts the turnaround in the southern region.
